★ High-risk prophylaxis or established infection → **amoxicillin-clavulanate**; severe infection → IV ampicillin-sulbactam
Prophylaxis usually 3–5 days; established infection needs longer, guided by depth and response
★ Hand punctures, infected wounds → **leave open**; selected clean facial lacerations → primary closure
Rabies-risk exposure: unvaccinated → wound HRIG + vaccine days 0, 3, 7, 14; immunocompromised add 28

rows.label: Complications
items: Tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia; asplenia → fulminant Capnocytophaga sepsis
Rabies almost universally fatal after symptoms begin

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Dirty wound: **tetanus booster if ≥5 years**; unknown/incomplete series → vaccine + TIG
Prior rabies vaccination → vaccine days 0, 3; no HRIG; public health assesses animal risk
Healthy dog/cat/ferret available → 10-day observation coordinated with public health; animal-handling education

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonbite cellulitis: no inoculation history or puncture
Crystal arthritis: joint inflammation with crystals, but aspiration still needed if infection possible

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery, incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Partial obstruction may still permit stool or diarrhea; bowel movements do not exclude early obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs

breast-neoplasia.name: Breast neoplasia
breast-neoplasia.scope: Ductal carcinoma in situ, invasive ductal and lobular carcinoma, receptor status (ER, PR, HER2), metastatic disease (bone, visceral), surgical management, endocrine and chemotherapy
breast-neoplasia.core: A suspicious breast lesion requires core biopsy, assessment of invasion and ER/PR/HER2 status to guide local and systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, BRCA-related syndromes, family history, prior chest irradiation
Prolonged estrogen exposure, postmenopausal obesity, alcohol; atypical proliferative breast lesions

rows.label: Clues
items: Painless hard irregular mass, skin/nipple retraction, unilateral bloody discharge or axillary node
★ Peau d’orange, diffuse erythema and edema → **inflammatory breast cancer**, even without discrete mass
Persistent unilateral eczematous nipple lesion → Paget disease; investigate underlying carcinoma

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Invasion through basement membrane enables lymphatic/hematogenous metastasis
ER/PR signaling and HER2 amplification create actionable tumor drivers; triple-negative tumors lack these targets

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diagnostic mammography + targeted ultrasound** → core needle biopsy of suspicious lesion
Pathology: invasion, grade, **ER/PR/HER2**; assess regional nodes clinically and with targeted imaging
Clinically node-negative invasive disease → sentinel node biopsy during definitive surgery
Distant staging scans for advanced disease or suspicious symptoms; not every small asymptomatic cancer

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early: lumpectomy + radiation or mastectomy; locally advanced: neoadjuvant systemic treatment then surgery/radiation
ER-positive → tamoxifen or postmenopausal aromatase inhibitor; chemotherapy based on stage/biology
★ HER2-positive → **trastuzumab-based** treatment; monitor LVEF
Triple-negative → chemotherapy; selected higher-risk disease → pembrolizumab-containing regimen
Bone metastases → **zoledronate/denosumab**; systemic treatment by receptors, chemotherapy for visceral crisis

rows.label: Complications
items: Metastases to bone, lung, liver, brain; surgery/radiation → lymphedema
Tamoxifen → VTE/endometrial cancer; aromatase inhibitors → bone loss; trastuzumab → cardiomyopathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Age/risk-based screening, genetic counseling for suggestive pedigree; selected high-risk patients → chemoprevention
BRCA-related very high risk → discuss risk-reducing surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mastitis: lactation-associated tenderness/fever, improves with antibiotics
Fat necrosis: trauma/surgery history; biopsy if discordant imaging

carotid-artery-stenosis.name: Carotid artery stenosis
carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia; coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Prior neck radiation increases stenosis and surgical complexity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Amaurosis fugax**, contralateral weakness/numbness, or aphasia → symptomatic disease
Bruit may be incidental; loudness does not measure severity, complete occlusion may be silent
Isolated dizziness or syncope rarely represents carotid-territory ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture → artery-to-artery emboli; critical narrowing can reduce cerebral perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected stenosis or selected incidental bruit evaluation → **carotid duplex ultrasound**
CTA/MRA confirms anatomy before intervention; brain imaging evaluates neurologic deficits
★ **No routine screening** of asymptomatic general adults; bruit auscultation is an unreliable screen

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Post-revascularization hyperperfusion syndrome → headache, seizures, intracerebral hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms

catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.name: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.scope: Central line infection, organisms, line removal, prevention
catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.core: Fever or rigors in a patient with an intravascular catheter, especially during infusion, raises concern for catheter-related bacteremia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long catheter dwell time, femoral placement, parenteral nutrition, immunosuppression, hemodialysis
Poor asepsis, frequent hub manipulation; tunneled devices and ports also susceptible

rows.label: Clues
items: Exit-site erythema or drainage may occur; normal insertion-site appearance does not exclude infection
★ **Hypotension, persistent bacteremia**, new murmur, or embolic signs → complicated infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Skin flora migrate externally or contaminated hubs seed intraluminal biofilm
Biofilm limits antibiotic penetration; S aureus and Candida frequently seed distant sites

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Before antibiotics: **paired peripheral and catheter blood cultures**, labelled by source
Same organism with catheter culture positive ≥2 h earlier supports catheter source
Culture removed catheter tip when infection suspected; no routine tip culture after elective removal
Repeat blood cultures to document clearance; persistent positivity → endocarditis, infected thrombus, abscess evaluation
S aureus bacteremia → echocardiography, TEE when high risk; assess metastatic foci

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sepsis → **IV vancomycin + cefepime**, adjusted to cultures and local resistance
★ **Remove line** for shock, tunnel infection, endocarditis, persistent bacteremia, S aureus, Pseudomonas, or fungi
Candida → echinocandin; MSSA → cefazolin or nafcillin; enterococcal treatment follows susceptibilities
Selected stable long-term line infections with coagulase-negative staphylococci → systemic antibiotics + antibiotic lock
Uncomplicated S aureus bacteremia: ≥14 days after clearance; endocarditis/deep infection usually requires 4–6 weeks

rows.label: Complications
items: Endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, osteomyelitis, septic emboli, shock
Unnecessary device retention → relapse; repeated placement → thrombosis and vascular injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Hand hygiene, chlorhexidine skin preparation, maximal sterile barrier** during insertion
Scrub hubs, sterile dressings, daily necessity review, prompt removal of unnecessary lines
Avoid routine prophylactic systemic antibiotics or scheduled catheter replacement solely to prevent infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contaminated blood culture: single skin-flora isolate without corroborating cultures or illness
Infusate reaction: temporal symptoms without reproducible bacteremia
Catheter thrombosis: swelling, poor flow; cultures negative unless infected

rows: Parenteral nutrition, broad antibiotics; remove catheter

cervical-spine-injury.name: Cervical spine injury
cervical-spine-injury.scope: Whiplash, cervical strain, NEXUS criteria, Canadian C-spine rule, cervical fractures (odontoid, hangman, burst), atlantoaxial subluxation, spinal clearance
cervical-spine-injury.core: After trauma, protect the neck until a reliable low-risk examination or imaging excludes clinically significant cervical injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-energy collision, axial load, falls in older adults; osteoporosis
Rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome → atlantoaxial instability

rows.label: Clues
items: Midline tenderness, paresthesias, weakness; high cord injury may impair ventilation
Whiplash: acceleration-deceleration injury with muscular pain and stiffness, usually no neurologic deficit

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fracture or ligament disruption → instability; secondary motion may injure spinal cord

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NEXUS**: alert; no intoxication, midline tenderness, focal deficit or distracting injury → clinical clearance
★ Canadian rule: **age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, or extremity paresthesias** → imaging
Low-risk features: simple rear-end collision, ambulatory, seated, delayed neck pain, or no midline tenderness
Low-risk feature present + active rotation 45° each way → clear; otherwise image
★ Imaging required → **CT cervical spine**; deficit or suspected ligament/cord injury → MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway with manual inline stabilization; immobilize suspected unstable injury and obtain spine consultation
Unstable fracture or cord compression → stabilization/decompression; avoid routine high-dose methylprednisolone
Uncomplicated strain after clearance: NSAIDs, early gentle mobilization and exercise; avoid prolonged soft-collar use
Negative high-quality CT usually permits collar removal without neurologic concern; discordant findings → spine consultation

rows.label: Complications
items: Spinal cord injury, respiratory failure, neurogenic shock; immobilization → pressure injury and stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seat belts, helmets, fall prevention; avoid axial loading during diving
★ **Do not force neck movement** in an unreliable examination or high-risk patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Muscular strain: paraspinal pain after dangerous injury excluded
Degenerative stenosis: chronic symptoms; may predispose to cord injury after minor trauma

clostridioides-difficile-infection.name: Clostridioides difficile infection
clostridioides-difficile-infection.scope: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, toxic megacolon, pseudomembranous colitis, NAAT vs EIA stool toxin testing, oral fidaxomicin, oral vancomycin, fulminant colitis
clostridioides-difficile-infection.core: Recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure followed by watery diarrhea suggests toxin-mediated colitis; ileus can conceal fulminant disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins; older age, hospitalization, immunosuppression
Prior infection and unnecessary acid suppression increase susceptibility or recurrence

rows.label: Clues
items: Abdominal cramps, fever, leukocytosis; severe disease may cause AKI and hypoalbuminemia
★ **Hypotension, ileus, or megacolon** defines fulminant infection; diarrhea may disappear

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Antibiotic disruption of microbiota permits spore-forming bacilli to proliferate
Toxins damage colonic epithelium → inflammation and pseudomembranes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Test **unformed stool** with ≥3 unexplained stools/24 hours; exclude laxative effect
NAAT detects toxigenic genes, not active toxin; positive results can represent colonization
Toxin EIA is less sensitive; multistep GDH/NAAT plus toxin improves clinical specificity
No test of cure; abdominal imaging for distention, toxicity, or suspected perforation

rows.label: Tx
items: Stop inciting antibiotic when possible; replace fluids/electrolytes, avoid antimotility drugs in severe colitis
★ Initial nonfulminant infection: **oral fidaxomicin** preferred; oral vancomycin acceptable, usually 10 days
★ Fulminant: **high-dose oral/NG vancomycin + IV metronidazole**; add rectal vancomycin with ileus
Shock, perforation, worsening organ failure → urgent surgical consultation
Recurrence: fidaxomicin or tapered/pulsed vancomycin; multiple recurrences → screened microbiota-based treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Toxic megacolon, perforation, sepsis, recurrent infection
Severe classification: WBC >15,000/µL or creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL; different from fulminant criteria

rows.label: Prevention
items: Contact precautions, gloves/gown, soap-and-water handwashing, sporicidal surface cleaning
Antibiotic stewardship; no screening/treatment of asymptomatic carriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Laxative-associated diarrhea: medication timing, no inflammatory syndrome
IBD flare: chronic relapsing course; test for coinfection before escalating immunosuppression

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts increase pulmonary flow; longstanding vascular remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell → knee–chest position, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; irreversible Eisenmenger physiology → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

constipation-and-fecal-impaction.name: Constipation and fecal impaction
constipation-and-fecal-impaction.scope: Functional constipation, medication-induced constipation, fecal impaction and overflow incontinence, digital disimpaction, laxatives, fiber
constipation-and-fecal-impaction.core: Difficult, infrequent, or incomplete defecation; loose stool can represent overflow around an impacted rectal stool mass.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low fiber, immobility, dehydration, withholding, older age; childhood onset often follows painful defecation/toilet training
Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, verapamil; hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, neurologic disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Hard/lumpy stool, straining, incomplete emptying, <3 spontaneous stools/week; frequency alone insufficient
★ **Rectal fullness, paradoxical diarrhea, fecal soiling, urinary retention** → consider impaction
★ **Bleeding, anemia, weight loss, new persistent change**, severe distension/vomiting → structural evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Slow transit increases water absorption; pelvic-floor dyssynergia prevents coordinated expulsion
Stool retention stretches rectum → reduced sensation and leakage of liquid around retained mass

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ History, drug review, abdominal examination, **digital rectal examination** for stool, masses, pelvic-floor dysfunction
No alarm findings → clinical diagnosis; targeted TSH/calcium if suspected; colonoscopy for alarms or overdue screening
Refractory despite laxatives → anorectal manometry + balloon-expulsion test; then transit studies if needed
Empty rectum does not exclude proximal impaction; obstruction concern → abdominal imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Palpable hard rectal mass → **manual disimpaction**, then enemas; proximal stool → PEG after obstruction excluded
★ Uncomplicated constipation → **fiber gradually + polyethylene glycol**; hydration if depleted, scheduled postmeal toileting
Dyssynergic defecation → pelvic-floor biofeedback; stool softener alone will not correct outlet dysfunction
Opioid-induced: stimulant + osmotic laxative; refractory → naloxegol/naldemedine after excluding bowel obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Anal fissures, hemorrhoids, prolapse, stercoral ulceration/perforation, recurrent impaction
Magnesium laxatives → hypermagnesemia in CKD; phosphate enemas → electrolyte injury, especially renal disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintenance bowel regimen after disimpaction; regular activity, adequate dietary fiber, minimize constipating drugs
Avoid bulk fiber during unresolved impaction; pediatric withholding → reward-based routine, no punishment

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS-C: recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation/stool changes
Bowel obstruction: colicky pain, vomiting, obstipation, dilated bowel
Hirschsprung: neonatal delayed meconium, distension, absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex

rows: Limited efficacy; avoid relying on it

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic cough/hoarseness nonspecific and often multifactorial
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional or acute chest pain requires cardiac evaluation before attributing symptoms to reflux

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with troublesome regurgitation despite optimized drugs → fundoplication or selected endoscopic intervention
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → endoscopic dilation plus acid suppression; dysplastic Barrett requires specialist eradication treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastrointestinal-perforation.name: Gastrointestinal perforation
gastrointestinal-perforation.scope: Gastroduodenal perforation, bowel perforation (diverticular, appendiceal, iatrogenic), pneumoperitoneum (subdiaphragmatic free air), acute peritonitis, IV antibiotics, emergent exploratory laparotomy
gastrointestinal-perforation.core: Abrupt severe abdominal pain with guarding, rigidity, and free intraperitoneal air suggests a perforated viscus requiring rapid resuscitation and source control.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Peptic ulcer disease, NSAIDs, H. pylori; diverticulitis, appendicitis, obstruction, ischemia, malignancy
Recent endoscopy/surgery, penetrating/blunt trauma; glucocorticoids/immunosuppression can blunt peritoneal findings

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, tachycardia, absent bowel sounds, distension; pain with movement/cough
★ **Hypotension, confusion, oliguria, elevated lactate** → septic shock/organ hypoperfusion
Retroperitoneal or contained leaks may lack diffuse rigidity or visible free air

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal contents spill into peritoneum → chemical inflammation followed by bacterial infection and sepsis
Fluid sequestration and vasodilation reduce effective circulating volume

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable patient → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** to localize leak and abscess
Upright chest radiograph: subdiaphragmatic free air; negative film does not exclude perforation
CBC, metabolic panel, lactate, blood cultures if septic, type/crossmatch; pregnancy test when relevant
★ **Unstable with generalized peritonitis → surgery**, without delaying for CT
Avoid barium studies or diagnostic endoscopy when perforation suspected; water-soluble contrast only for selected questions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, large-bore IVs, isotonic crystalloid**, analgesia; immediate surgical consultation
★ Prompt **piperacillin-tazobactam** or ceftriaxone + metronidazole; cover enteric gram-negatives/anaerobes
Nasogastric decompression for upper GI leak/ileus; IV proton-pump inhibitor for ulcer perforation
Urgent operative repair/resection and washout for free perforation; norepinephrine if shock persists after fluids
Selected stable contained leak may receive antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage with close surgical observation

rows.label: Complications
items: Intra-abdominal abscess, septic shock, multiorgan failure, fistula; anastomotic leak after repair

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H. pylori after ulcer disease; avoid unnecessary NSAIDs, use gastroprotection when ulcer risk high
Treat causal disease, optimize postoperative leak recognition; reassess persistent fever/pain after procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pancreatitis: elevated lipase, characteristic epigastric/back pain without typical pneumoperitoneum
Mesenteric ischemia: initially pain out of proportion; later peritonitis indicates necrosis/perforation
Postoperative free air: may be expected, but instability/peritonitis demands leak evaluation

genitourinary-trauma.name: Genitourinary trauma
genitourinary-trauma.scope: Posterior urethral injury, anterior urethral injury, bladder rupture, retrograde urethrography, renal trauma, testicular trauma
genitourinary-trauma.core: Hematuria or inability to void after trauma requires localization of urinary injury before instrumentation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pelvic fracture → posterior urethra/bladder; straddle injury → anterior bulbar urethra
Deceleration, flank impact or penetrating wounds → renal/collecting-system injury
Blunt scrotal trauma → testicular rupture; empty bladder better protected than distended bladder

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Blood at urethral meatus**, retention or perineal hematoma → urethral injury
Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture → suspect bladder rupture
Flank ecchymosis, tenderness or lower rib fractures suggest renal injury
Scrotal swelling, bruising and loss of normal contour suggest testicular rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pelvic shearing disrupts membranous urethra; direct compression splits the bulbar segment
Intraperitoneal urine leakage irritates peritoneum; blood loss can cause shock despite modest hematuria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected urethral injury → **retrograde urethrogram before Foley**; no blind repeated attempts
★ Stable gross hematuria + pelvic fracture → **retrograde CT/plain cystography**
Renal concern, stable → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis with delayed images; microscopic hematuria plus hypotension qualifies
Normal hematuria assessment cannot exclude renal vascular injury after high-energy deceleration
Testicular injury → Doppler ultrasound; high clinical suspicion should not delay exploration

rows.label: Tx
items: Hemodynamic instability → trauma resuscitation and urgent operative/angiographic hemorrhage control
Urethral disruption → urology, suprapubic drainage or selected endoscopic realignment
★ **Intraperitoneal bladder rupture → surgical repair**; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture → catheter drainage
Stable renal injuries → observation; ongoing arterial bleeding → selective embolization
Testicular rupture → urgent exploration, repair and removal of nonviable tissue

rows.label: Complications
items: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence; urinary extravasation → infection or urinoma
Delayed renal bleeding, hypertension or kidney loss; testicular atrophy and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective equipment; safe catheter technique; follow-up for stricture after urethral injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: absent flow with spermatic-cord twist; also surgical emergency
Nontraumatic stone: colicky flank pain without injury mechanism

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles, dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Start beta-blocker only when compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI requires 36-hour washout
MRA requires eGFR >30, K <5; persistent EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

hemolytic-anemias.name: Hemolytic Anemias
hemolytic-anemias.scope: autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm and cold agglutinins), hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, DAT/Coombs testing, peripheral smear, complications
hemolytic-anemias.core: Reticulocytosis, elevated LDH/indirect bilirubin and reduced haptoglobin suggest hemolysis; DAT and smear identify the mechanism.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune disease, CLL, drugs → immune hemolysis; infections can trigger cold-antibody disease
Family history → inherited membrane/enzyme defect; oxidants, fava beans or infection trigger G6PD crises

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dark urine; splenomegaly suggests chronic extravascular destruction
Severe intravascular lysis → hemoglobinuria, back pain, AKI; hemoglobin decline can outpace reticulocyte response
Spherocytes occur in hereditary and warm immune disease; morphology alone cannot distinguish them

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extravascular: splenic/hepatic macrophage clearance; intravascular: RBC destruction within circulation
Free hemoglobin consumes haptoglobin; marrow compensates unless infection, deficiency or marrow failure limits production

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin**, peripheral smear
★ **DAT/Coombs** detects immune coating; negative test redirects toward nonimmune causes
Hereditary spherocytosis → eosin-5-maleimide binding test; ↑MCHC supports
G6PD activity can be falsely normal during crisis/after transfusion → repeat after recovery
Schistocytes → evaluate microangiopathy/mechanical destruction urgently, including platelet count and renal function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe symptomatic anemia → **transfuse promptly** with blood-bank coordination; do not await perfect compatibility
Warm AIHA → glucocorticoids; refractory → rituximab or selected splenectomy
Cold disease → warmth, treat cause; rituximab-based treatment when symptomatic; steroids usually ineffective
G6PD → stop oxidant, treat trigger, supportive transfusion when severe
Hereditary spherocytosis → folate; selected severe disease → splenectomy after immunization

rows.label: Complications
items: Pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, aplastic crisis; chronic immune disease increases thrombosis risk
Splenectomy → encapsulated infection and thrombosis; intravascular disease → renal injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ G6PD: avoid **dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase** and other oxidants
Before splenectomy: pneumococcal/meningococcal/Hib vaccines; infection education and selected antibiotic prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blood loss: reticulocytosis without hemolytic chemistry
Gilbert syndrome: isolated indirect bilirubin without anemia

table.title: Mechanism signatures
rows: Bite cells; Heinz bodies on supravital stain

hemolytic-anemias.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology teaching.

hepatic-masses.name: Hepatic masses
hepatic-masses.scope: Hepatic hemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia (central scar), hepatic adenoma (OCP risk), hepatocellular carcinoma, liver metastases, triphasic CT or MRI, resection indications
hepatic-masses.core: An incidental liver lesion is classified by liver disease, cancer history, and dynamic contrast enhancement before biopsy or surgery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HCC: cirrhosis, chronic HBV even without cirrhosis; metastases: known extrahepatic malignancy
Adenoma: estrogen-containing OCPs, anabolic steroids, obesity, glycogen storage disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Most benign lesions asymptomatic; RUQ pain, early satiety, weight loss require assessment
★ Sudden pain, hypotension, falling hemoglobin → **ruptured hemorrhagic lesion**
New decompensation or portal-vein tumor thrombus in cirrhosis raises concern for HCC

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hemangioma: vascular spaces; FNH: hyperplastic response around abnormal artery with functioning hepatocytes
Adenoma: hepatocellular proliferation lacking normal bile ducts; HCC: malignant hepatocytes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Indeterminate lesion → **multiphase contrast CT or MRI**; hepatobiliary MRI distinguishes FNH from adenoma
AFP supports HCC but normal values do not exclude it; not diagnostic alone
At-risk liver with characteristic HCC imaging → diagnosis often without biopsy; atypical lesions → tissue assessment
Avoid biopsy of suspected hemangioma because of bleeding risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Asymptomatic hemangioma/FNH → reassurance; selected liver-limited colorectal metastases → resection
★ Adenoma: stop exogenous hormones, reduce weight; men → resection regardless of size
Women: persistent ≥5 cm, growth, or high-risk features → resection after risk-factor modification
Ruptured adenoma → resuscitate then arterial embolization; smaller stable lesions → imaging surveillance
HCC: preserved liver → resection; eligible cirrhosis → transplant; alternatives: ablation, atezolizumab/bevacizumab

rows.label: Complications
items: Adenoma: hemorrhage, malignant transformation; large hemangioma rarely causes consumptive coagulopathy
Malignancy: vascular invasion, hepatic failure, distant spread

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Cirrhosis/selected chronic HBV → liver ultrasound + AFP every 6 months
HBV vaccination, HBV/HCV treatment, reduced alcohol exposure; address metabolic liver disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Liver abscess: fever, leukocytosis, rim-enhancing fluid lesion
Simple cyst: anechoic, thin-walled, posterior acoustic enhancement

table.title: Imaging patterns
rows: Arterial enhancement; usually hepatobiliary contrast defect
Often multiple; enhancement depends on primary

hiatal-hernia.name: Hiatal hernia
hiatal-hernia.scope: Sliding hiatal hernia, paraesophageal hiatal hernia, gastric volvulus risk, barium swallow, surgical repair
hiatal-hernia.core: Herniation of stomach through the diaphragmatic hiatus causes reflux or mechanical obstruction; volvulus and ischemia require urgent surgical care.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age-related diaphragmatic laxity, obesity, pregnancy, increased intra-abdominal pressure; connective-tissue weakness
Prior foregut surgery may predispose to recurrent or altered hiatal anatomy

rows.label: Clues
items: Heartburn, regurgitation, positional symptoms; large hernias → dysphagia, early satiety or postprandial chest pressure
Chronic occult blood loss from Cameron erosions → iron-deficiency anemia
★ Severe epigastric pain, **unproductive retching, inability to pass NG tube** → gastric volvulus
Dyspnea or recurrent aspiration can indicate symptomatic large paraesophageal disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hiatal widening permits proximal stomach migration; disrupted antireflux barrier promotes acid exposure
Rotation/entrapment of intrathoracic stomach compromises outflow and potentially perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Barium swallow** defines anatomy and rotation; endoscopy evaluates mucosal injury/anemia
Acute severe symptoms → contrast CT for obstruction, ischemia or perforation
Before elective antireflux surgery → manometry; reflux monitoring when objective GERD evidence absent
Chest radiograph may show retrocardiac air-fluid level; cannot fully characterize complications

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Reflux-predominant sliding hernia → **PPI**, weight loss, smaller meals, head-of-bed elevation
Persistent objectively confirmed reflux or complications → selected surgical repair/fundoplication
Symptomatic paraesophageal hernia → elective repair after operative-risk assessment
★ Volvulus, strangulation or perforation → resuscitation, decompression and **urgent surgery**
Truly asymptomatic paraesophageal hernia → shared decision about repair versus surveillance

rows.label: Complications
items: Esophagitis, stricture, Barrett esophagus; mechanical obstruction, gastric necrosis, hemorrhage
Repair → recurrence, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome

rows.label: Prevention
items: Weight management, avoid late meals; smoking cessation reduces reflux burden
Known unrepaired paraesophageal hernia → counsel on emergency obstructive symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: ACS: ischemic ECG/troponin findings; exclude with suspicious acute chest symptoms
Achalasia: impaired LES relaxation and esophageal retention without primary hiatal migration

hyperbilirubinemia.name: Hyperbilirubinemia
hyperbilirubinemia.scope: Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, unconjugated vs conjugated, biliary atresia
hyperbilirubinemia.core: Fractionate bilirubin first: indirect elevation reflects production or conjugation problems; direct elevation requires assessment of hepatobiliary excretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fasting, illness or dehydration triggers Gilbert jaundice; family history suggests inherited bilirubin disorders
Persistent infant jaundice can reflect biliary atresia even after initially reassuring appearance

rows.label: Clues
items: Indirect bilirubin is albumin-bound and absent from urine; direct bilirubin can darken urine
★ Infant **pale/acholic stools**, dark urine, hepatomegaly → obstructive cholestasis
Pruritus, pale stools and elevated alkaline phosphatase suggest impaired bile flow
Severe neonatal indirect elevation with lethargy, poor feeding or abnormal tone → bilirubin neurotoxicity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heme breakdown yields unconjugated pigment; hepatic UGT conjugation enables biliary elimination
Unbound unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood–brain barrier; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Total/direct bilirubin**, AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase/GGT; CBC/reticulocytes/LDH for suspected hemolysis
Isolated mild indirect elevation with normal liver tests and no hemolysis → Gilbert diagnosis
★ Jaundice beyond 2 weeks → fractionate; **direct ≥1 mg/dL at 2–4 weeks** → urgent referral
Infant cholestasis → ultrasound; biliary atresia assessment may require biopsy and operative cholangiography
Adult conjugated elevation with pain/obstruction → RUQ ultrasound before advanced duct imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected biliary atresia → urgent pediatric hepatology/surgery; **early Kasai portoenterostomy**
Severe neonatal indirect elevation → age/gestation/risk-based phototherapy; exchange transfusion at critical thresholds
Crigler–Najjar I → intensive phototherapy, definitive liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital
Gilbert, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor → reassurance once competing pathology excluded
Cholestasis → nutritional support, fat-soluble vitamins and cause-specific treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Indirect neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → acute encephalopathy/kernicterus
Untreated atresia → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Inspect stool color and fractionate persistent infant jaundice; never label conjugated jaundice physiologic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin
Choledochal cyst: cystic/dilated extrahepatic ducts on ultrasound

hyperbilirubinemia.evidence: Infant referral checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2025](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/pdfDownload/31302); inherited syndromes established teaching.

hypercalcemia.name: Hypercalcemia
hypercalcemia.scope: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, milk-alkali syndrome, IV saline resuscitation, calcitonin, bisphosphonates
hypercalcemia.core: Elevated calcium causes stones, constipation, polyuria, weakness, and neuropsychiatric changes; PTH distinguishes hormone-driven disease from other causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia, malignancy, prolonged immobilization
Thiazides, lithium, excess vitamin D or calcium/absorbable alkali, granulomatous disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Dehydration, nausea, abdominal pain, reduced reflexes; ECG may show shortened QT
★ **Calcium >14 mg/dL**, confusion, arrhythmia, or severe volume depletion → urgent treatment
Primary hyperparathyroidism often asymptomatic; malignancy-associated disease tends to progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PTH promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention while increasing phosphate excretion
Hypercalcemia impairs renal concentration → dehydration, reduced calcium clearance, self-reinforcing elevation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm with repeat total/albumin-adjusted or **ionized calcium**, especially with altered proteins or critical illness
★ **Intact PTH first**; elevated or inappropriately normal → PTH-dependent
Suppressed PTH → PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, malignancy/myeloma evaluation guided by context
Primary disease versus FHH → urine calcium; clearance ratio <0.01 favors FHH, with overlap
Parathyroid imaging localizes before surgery; never establishes biochemical diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe/symptomatic → **IV isotonic saline**, then calcitonin for rapid temporary lowering
★ **IV zoledronic acid** for sustained malignancy control; denosumab if severe renal limitations/refractory disease
Calcitriol-mediated disease → glucocorticoids; dialysis for refractory life-threatening elevation or inability to hydrate
Primary disease: surgery for symptoms, age <50, calcium >1 above ULN, osteoporosis/fracture, stones, eGFR <60
Stop causative supplements/drugs; loop diuretic only for fluid overload, not routine calcium elimination

rows.label: Complications
items: Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, AKI, osteoporosis/fractures, pancreatitis
Calcitonin tachyphylaxis after 48–72 hours; antiresorptives can cause hypocalcemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration, avoid excess calcium/alkali; monitor calcium, renal function, and bone density when observing primary disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: FHH: lifelong mild elevation, family history, hypocalciuria; surgery ineffective
Pseudohypercalcemia: high protein-bound calcium but normal ionized fraction

hypercalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established calcium evaluation and emergency management.

hypocalcemia.name: Hypocalcemia
hypocalcemia.scope: Hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, post-thyroidectomy, hypomagnesemia
hypocalcemia.core: Low ionized calcium causes neuromuscular irritability and QT prolongation; severe symptoms require IV calcium while the cause is corrected.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge syndrome
Vitamin D deficiency from low intake, malabsorption, limited sun; CKD, pancreatitis, massive citrate transfusion
Severe hypomagnesemia from alcoholism, diarrhea, PPIs, diuretics; bisphosphonates/denosumab can precipitate deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Perioral tingling, distal paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm
★ **Trousseau sign**: cuff-induced carpal spasm; Chvostek sign is less specific
★ Severe: **seizures, laryngospasm, arrhythmias**; ECG shows prolonged QT
Post-thyroidectomy tingling or stridor requires immediate calcium assessment rather than simple reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers nerve excitation threshold; myocardial repolarization is prolonged
Low magnesium impairs both PTH secretion and action, making calcium replacement alone ineffective

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ionized calcium**, Mg, phosphate, creatinine, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Low albumin lowers total calcium, not necessarily ionized; correction formulas unreliable in critical illness
Alkalosis increases albumin binding → symptomatic low ionized calcium despite unchanged total concentration
Interpret PTH relative to calcium: normal PTH can be inappropriately low during hypocalcemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic, severe, or ECG changes → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**
Mild stable disease → oral calcium; nutritional vitamin D deficiency → cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol
Hypoparathyroidism or advanced CKD → **calcitriol** plus calcium; coordinate phosphate management
★ **Replace magnesium** when deficient; correct underlying cause, avoid overcorrection

rows.label: Complications
items: Tetany, seizures, ventricular arrhythmias; chronic deficiency can cause cataracts and basal ganglia calcification
Overreplacement → hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis; monitor serum and urine calcium

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor calcium after neck surgery and antiresorptive treatment; ensure sufficient vitamin D/calcium intake
Chronic hypoparathyroidism: target symptom control with low-normal serum calcium, avoiding renal calcium loading

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperventilation syndrome: transient alkalosis-related ionized reduction; assess precipitating illness
Seizure disorder: no biochemical calcium explanation; pseudohypocalcemia: normal ionized level

hypocalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching.

hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
hypothyroidism.scope: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subclinical hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, autoimmune associations, levothyroxine dosing, TSH monitoring
hypothyroidism.core: Insufficient thyroid hormone slows metabolism, causing fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and delayed reflex relaxation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hashimoto autoimmunity, thyroid surgery/radioiodine, iodine deficiency/excess
Lithium, amiodarone, postpartum thyroiditis; pituitary surgery/radiation or mass

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight gain, bradycardia, hoarseness, heavy menses, hyperlipidemia; hyponatremia in severe disease
★ **Hypothermia, altered mentation, hypoventilation, hypotension** → myxedema coma
Autoimmune clustering: type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, celiac disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced hormone activity lowers thermogenesis and cardiac output; glycosaminoglycan deposition produces nonpitting edema
Hashimoto: lymphocytic destruction; anti-TPO antibodies support autoimmune cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH and free T4** establish hormone deficiency and localize the level of dysfunction
Positive anti-TPO predicts progression from subclinical disease; ultrasound unnecessary without nodule/goiter concern
Recheck mild isolated TSH elevation after transient illness resolves; exclude medication interference

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Levothyroxine**; healthy young adult approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; older/CAD start 12.5–25 mcg/day
Take fasting; separate calcium/iron; reassess TSH about 6–8 weeks after changes
Central disease: titrate using free T4; evaluate/replace cortisol before thyroid hormone
Subclinical: generally treat TSH ≥10; consider symptoms, antibodies, pregnancy at lower values
★ Myxedema: **IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone**, airway support, cautious fluids/passive warming; treat trigger

rows.label: Complications
items: Dyslipidemia, infertility, pericardial effusion, neuropathy; severe disease → respiratory failure
Excess replacement → AF, angina, bone loss; rapid correction in CAD can precipitate ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Pregnancy: early **TSH monitoring**, usually increase existing replacement promptly; use pregnancy-specific targets
Monitor stable replacement at least annually; address adherence/absorption before escalating doses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Depression: mood symptoms without thyroid biochemical pattern
Euthyroid sick syndrome: acute systemic illness, often low T3; avoid routine hormone replacement

hypothyroidism.evidence: Not checked online; established thyroid replacement and endocrine emergency teaching.

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late dangerous finding
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings, normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway support, head elevation, IV hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum; PSC particularly associated with UC
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention suggests **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Steroids induce remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas, strictures, obstruction and B12 deficiency in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate, reason, communicate choice**; specific to decision, fluctuating
Competence: legal determination; diagnosis, age, or disagreement alone does not establish incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, including life-saving treatment; avoid coercion or abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no available surrogate/directive → implied consent for necessary treatment
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or substantially changed risk → renewed consent discussion

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

meckel-diverticulum.name: Meckel diverticulum
meckel-diverticulum.scope: Persistent vitelline duct, ectopic gastric mucosa, painless lower GI bleeding, technetium-99m pertechnetate scan, intussusception, surgical resection
meckel-diverticulum.core: A congenital ileal remnant can present with childhood intestinal bleeding, obstruction, or appendicitis-like inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Persistent **vitelline/omphalomesenteric duct**; congenital lesion, symptomatic disease more common in boys
Ectopic gastric tissue increases bleeding; complications often arise in childhood, but possible at any age

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Painless maroon or bright-red rectal bleeding** in an otherwise well child
Colicky pain, vomiting or obstruction when serving as an intussusception lead point
Diverticulitis → fever, RLQ pain and tenderness; perforation produces peritoneal signs
Large-volume blood loss → pallor, tachycardia or shock; benign abdominal examination does not ensure mild disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: True diverticulum contains all bowel-wall layers, usually antimesenteric distal ileum
Acid secretion from heterotopic gastric mucosa ulcerates adjacent ileal lining

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected bleeding Meckel → **technetium-99m pertechnetate scan**, detects gastric mucosa
Negative scan does not exclude lesion without sufficient ectopic tissue; pediatric sensitivity exceeds adult sensitivity
Ultrasound if intussusception suspected; CT for inflammatory/obstructive presentations or alternative diagnoses
CBC, type/crossmatch for substantial bleeding; endoscopic studies may be unrevealing because lesion lies beyond routine reach

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Brisk bleeding/shock → **IV access, crystalloid/blood**, urgent pediatric/surgical consultation
★ Symptomatic lesion → **diverticulectomy or segmental ileal resection**, including adjacent ulcerated bowel
Perforation/peritonitis → broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent operation; obstruction → NPO and decompression
Incidentally found asymptomatic lesion → individualized surgical decision based on risk and operative context

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent hemorrhage and anemia, intussusception, volvulus around fibrous band, bowel ischemia
Diverticulitis or perforation; postoperative adhesions can cause later small-bowel obstruction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Juvenile polyp: painless bleeding but intraluminal colonic lesion on colonoscopy
Anal fissure: painful stooling with surface streaks; peptic bleeding: upper-GI source

meckel-diverticulum.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

occupational-lung-disease.name: Occupational lung disease
occupational-lung-disease.scope: Silicosis, asbestosis, coal workers' pneumoconiosis, berylliosis
occupational-lung-disease.core: Progressive exertional dyspnea and interstitial lung abnormalities years after dust exposure require a detailed occupational history and exposure-specific imaging interpretation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cumulative inhaled mineral dust, inadequate respiratory protection, mining/construction/manufacturing exposures
Long latency permits disease after retirement; smoking adds obstructive disease and cancer risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Dry cough, exertional breathlessness, reduced exercise capacity; examination may show crackles
Advanced disease: resting hypoxemia, cyanosis, clubbing or right-heart strain
Pleural plaques mark exposure but often do not explain substantial functional impairment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Persistent particles activate macrophages and profibrotic pathways → irreversible interstitial scarring
Beryllium triggers a delayed cellular immune response with noncaseating granulomas

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Detailed job/task history + chest imaging**; HRCT clarifies radiograph findings
PFTs often restrictive with reduced DLCO; obstructive or mixed patterns can occur
★ Beryllium suspicion → **beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test**; biopsy may show granulomas
★ Silica exposure → **TB assessment**; evaluate fever, weight loss, cavitation for active infection
New unilateral pleural effusion, nodular pleural thickening, or mass → malignancy workup, tissue diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Stop further exposure**, smoking cessation; oxygen for hypoxemia, pulmonary rehabilitation
Vaccination and prompt infection treatment; bronchodilators if coexisting airflow obstruction
Symptomatic progressive berylliosis → systemic glucocorticoids; no proven reversal of established dust fibrosis
Advanced refractory respiratory failure → lung transplant evaluation; treat TB or cancer separately

rows.label: Complications
items: Progressive massive fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure
Asbestos: bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma; smoking synergizes lung carcinoma risk, not mesothelioma
Silicosis: TB/nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, lung cancer

rows.label: Prevention
items: Engineering dust controls, wet cutting, fitted respirators, occupational surveillance
Protect household contacts from contaminated work clothing; adherence to workplace exposure limits

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sarcoidosis: granulomas without relevant exposure; beryllium test negative
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: basal subpleural honeycombing without causative occupational history
Heart failure: congestion/effusions with cardiac dysfunction

occupational-lung-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established occupational pulmonary medicine teaching.

palliative-and-hospice-care.name: Palliative and hospice care
palliative-and-hospice-care.scope: Hospice eligibility, pain control, goals of care, surrogate requests
palliative-and-hospice-care.core: Palliative care relieves suffering at any illness stage; hospice centers care on comfort when prognosis and patient goals support a terminal-care benefit.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Patient goals and informed consent** guide intervention burdens; symptom relief remains an obligation
Proportionate opioids for pain/dyspnea ethically permissible despite foreseeable unintended risks

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Ask understanding/values → discuss prognosis → recommend a goal-concordant plan
Assess capacity; use advance directive, then authorized surrogate: substituted judgment/best interests
★ Titrate **opioids** to symptoms; add stimulant laxative for constipation, reassess sedation/respiration

rows.label: Don't
items: DNR ≠ no antibiotics, fluids, nutrition or other desired treatment
Capable patient’s informed wishes override surrogate requests
No nonbeneficial interventions; explain reasoning, offer alternatives, seek ethics review for conflict

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Refractory terminal suffering → proportional palliative sedation, specialist review and consent
Emergency, unknown preferences → stabilize while clarifying wishes; honor documented refusals

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Hospice: **≤6-month prognosis** if usual course; longer survival permits recertification
Medicare hospice election concerns terminal-illness treatment; unrelated conditions remain treatable
No DNR requirement for hospice; enrollment can be revoked if goals change

palliative-and-hospice-care.evidence: Eligibility checked 2026-10-30: [CMS hospice benefit](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice); clinical ethics: established teaching.

pancreatic-cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic-cancer.scope: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, painless jaundice, Courvoisier sign, CA 19-9, neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma)
pancreatic-cancer.core: Older adult with weight loss and painless obstructive jaundice, or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, increasing age; strong family history, hereditary cancer syndromes
New diabetes with unexplained weight loss can signal occult malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Head lesions: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, nontender palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier sign**)
Body/tail lesions: late presentation with pain and cachexia; migratory thrombophlebitis may occur

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ductal adenocarcinoma causes biliary obstruction, perineural invasion, and early metastatic spread
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from endocrine cells; may be functional or incidental

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pancreatic-protocol CT** for mass, vessels, metastases; ultrasound may initially show biliary dilation
EUS biopsy before systemic treatment/uncertain diagnosis; not mandatory before straightforward resection
★ **CA 19-9** monitors disease; neither screening nor definitive diagnosis; obstruction can falsely elevate
Resectability depends on metastases and major vascular involvement; MRI clarifies indeterminate liver lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable head tumor → **Whipple**; body/tail tumor → distal pancreatectomy; add systemic chemotherapy
Borderline resectable → neoadjuvant treatment; metastatic → systemic treatment and palliation
★ Cholangitis → **urgent ERCP**; unresectable symptomatic jaundice → biliary stent
Analgesia, pancreatic enzymes for malabsorption, nutritional support

rows.label: Complications
items: VTE, biliary infection, gastric outlet obstruction, exocrine insufficiency, diabetes
Resection → pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, malabsorption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; no average-risk population screening; selected hereditary high-risk patients → MRI/EUS surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: colicky pain, ductal stone
Autoimmune pancreatitis: IgG4 elevation, diffuse pancreatic enlargement
Chronic pancreatitis: calcification, recurrent pain, prior inflammation

table.title: Functional neuroendocrine tumors
rows: ↑Insulin/C-peptide during supervised fast; negative sulfonylurea screen
